items.title: Female Reproductive Cycle - The Menstrual Cycle

source_refs.note: Topic 17.1.3 as printed: the three phase headings, both For Information boxes (menopause, hCG) (PDF 79-80); Figures 17.6 and 17.7 are original diagrams. The chapter's exercises (PDF 81-82) are not part of the lesson body.

blocks.text: The female reproductive system functions by going through cyclic events, collectively called the menstrual cycle. The menstrual cycle lasts approximately one month (28 days on average). It can be divided into the following phases.

In this phase, the functional layer of endometrium is shed. The detached tissue and blood move out of the body. This step is called menstruation. It continues for 3-5 days. It occurs due to low levels of estrogen and progesterone hormones. The gonadotropins and FSH begin to rise in this phase.

Due to the rise in FSH, few ovarian follicles begin growing. But, only one follicle grows full and the others degenerate. This mature follicle is called Graafian follicle rises to the surface of the ovary.

FSH stimulates the Graafian follicle to secrete estrogen hormones. It causes the initial vascularization of endometrium and makes it velvety and thick again. As the concentration of estrogen rises, the level of FSH falls due to negative feedback. Due to the fall in FSH level, the anterior pituitary releases LH. It happens at the end of the proliferative stage (day 14). The sudden release of LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates Graafian follicle to release the ovum into the oviduct. This phase is known as ovulation.

blocks.alt: Section of an ovary with blood vessels entering at the left. Stages are arranged clockwise, with arrows outside: primary follicles with primary oocytes, developing follicles growing a fluid space, a large Graafian follicle with its secondary oocyte, a ruptured follicle with the released ovum leaving the ovary, then early corpus luteum, corpus luteum and corpus luteum regressed.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.6: Changes in ovary during menstrual cycle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.6).

blocks.text: After ovulation, LH stimulates the ruptured Graafian follicle to develop into a yellow structure called the corpus luteum. Copus luteum secretes estrogen and progesterone hormones which make the endometrium more vascular and glandular.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “Copus luteum” is a misprint for corpus luteum, named in the sentence before.

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text: In human females, menstrual cycle stops around 50 year of age and it is termed as menopause.

If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum starts to degenerate. As a result, the anterior pituitary stops secreting LH. The destruction of corpus luteum also results in an abrupt fall in the concentration of estrogen and progesterone. It causes the thickened endometrium to be shed with bleeding i.e., menstruation on day 28.

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text: When the ovulated oocyte is fertilized, the tiny embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). This hormone maintains the corpus luteum. So, the levels of estrogen and progesterone keep high and menstruation is prevented. Because hCG comes from the embryonic chorion and not the mother, it is the hormone that is tested for in all pregnancy tests.

blocks.alt: Chart of days 0 to 28 in three rows, divided into the menstrual phase, follicular phase, ovulation at day 14 and secretory phase. Ovary: a follicle grows, ruptures at ovulation, becomes a corpus luteum and regresses. Hormone levels: FSH rises early with a small peak at ovulation; estrogen peaks just before ovulation and again around day 21; LH surges at day 13 to 14; progesterone peaks around day 22. Endometrium: shed in the first days, then thickens until late in the cycle.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.7: Menstrual cycle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.7; phase label spelled 'Secretory', menstrual phase line at day 5).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 17.7 labels 'Secretary phase' and ends the menstrual phase at day 4. The correct label is secretory phase, and the menstrual phase lasts days 1 to 5, as the book's text says; the drawing above shows both.
